# Broadcom Strategy and Business Model

## Executive Overview

Broadcom is a global semiconductor and infrastructure software company whose current form was created when Avago acquired Broadcom Corporation in 2016 and later adopted the Broadcom name. Headquartered in Palo Alto, California, Broadcom sells mission-critical technology into data centers, enterprise IT, broadband and telecom networks, smartphones, storage systems, and industrial markets. Its semiconductor portfolio spans custom artificial intelligence (AI) accelerators, Ethernet switching and routing silicon, broadband access chips, radio-frequency and wireless connectivity components, and storage connectivity products. Its software portfolio includes VMware virtualization and private-cloud platforms, mainframe software, cybersecurity, and application and network management products.

Broadcom’s strategy is unusually focused. Rather than trying to cover all of technology, it prefers a limited set of infrastructure layers where deep engineering, large design wins, switching costs, and disciplined cost control can support strong margins and cash generation. The company serves customers globally, with outsourced semiconductor manufacturing concentrated in Asia and software customers distributed across the Americas, Europe, and Asia-Pacific. For fiscal 2024, ended November 3, 2024, Broadcom reported revenue of $51.6 billion, with the VMware acquisition making infrastructure software a much larger part of the mix and increasing the share of recurring revenue.

TAIPEI, Taiwan--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Today at Computex 2026, Intel unveiled new innovations that address customers’ chip-to-systems-level AI needs with solutions tailored to address their specific industry challenges, including:

* **PC, gaming handheld, and physical AI momentum:** Broad partner support and customer uptake for the Series 3 family of processors.

According to Creative Strategies CEO and principal analyst Ben Bajarin, while “the training-era world looked closer to a one-CPU-per-four-GPU relation in AI deployments, agentic inference changes that relationship to roughly a one-CPU-to-one-GPU (or less) ratio.”

Seeking to capitalize on this trend at a systems level, Intel, SambaNova, and Foxconn today announced their intent to build rackscale AI infrastructure for data center, hyperscale, and intelligence center deployments—built on Intel Xeon processors.

The companies are demonstrating production-ready racks that combine Intel Xeon processors with SambaNova SN-50 RDUs, which together are designed to deliver high performance AI inference with improved cost and power efficiency. As part of the collaboration, Foxconn will provide system integration capabilities for the new rackscale AI infrastructure. Foxconn also plans to manufacture a CPU-dense variant of the rackscale infrastructure for workloads that do not require additional acceleration, including cost-optimized inference, data processing, and hybrid AI.
